Ah, I understand what you mean. But this line of code doesn't change anything from how it was working before.

Also:

1. Apple's Hazard Tracking is more like Vulkan Barriers, but they're related since render graphs were written to minimize the barriers.
2. Dario was the one who wrote the render graph, not me :smile: 
3. Hazard tracking is problematic for resources that need write access. If resource needs write access in command A, and read or write access in command B, then Metal must insert a barrier between A and B, so B doesn't start too early.
4. Before UMA, we always required write access so that the Copy Encoder can write from Staging into the Const/Storage buffers. Then the resource would be used (typically in read only, actually I'm 99% sure all dynamic buffers right now are read-only). Obviously this means serialization must happen between the end of the Copy Encoder and the start of the Render Encoder. It also means that for the next frame, serialization must happen between this frame's end of the Render Encoder and the next frame's beginning of Copy Enc. However this rarely is an issue for individual buffers because we're almost 99% certain a copy encoder and render encoder are needed.
5. After UMA, the situation improves dramatically, because no GPU command ever writes to these dynamic buffers (although I'm 1% not sure about storage dynamic buffers); thus there should be no need to serialize cmds (at least based on these buffers; but likely cmds are serialized nonetheless due to other unrelated copy operations).

Metal [docs](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/metal/mtlhazardtrackingmode/tracked) are very specific in their language: "If you submit a command that **modifies** the resource, Metal delays that command from executing until prior commands accessing that resource are complete" (emphasis mine).

"Modifies" means write access.

Turning off tracking actually still helps, but not because of GPU serialization, but because now the CPU has less overhead tracking what is being used on what, to see if that resource is ever used for write access. We can simply say "bro, trust me. It's always read only". Of course it's only faster if our implementation of barriers are better than what Metal does internally :laughing: .

How is that we never write to the buffer? Actually we never write to the buffer from the GPU. We do it from the CPU! This also needs a different kind of synchronization, and we ensure there are no race conditions due to the mechanism behind `rendering/rendering_device/vsync/frame_queue_size`, more specifically in `RenderingDevice::_begin_frame` we always call `_stall_for_frame`.

That's why dynamic buffers only bind a fragment of the buffer: `buf_info->frame_idx * buf_info->metal_buffer.length`.

Hi!

`UNIFORM_TYPE_UNIFORM_BUFFER_DYNAMIC` is exposed because API users _might_ receive a buffer created by Godot that requires this flag. In an ideal world we'd want API users to not even be aware of this type. But the API is too raw (a complaint/observation I raised internally in a channel: because Godot internally uses the same API that is exposed to API users, it creates friction when performance is needed over having a hand-holding safe API).

However API users cannot create such buffers because the flag `BUFFER_CREATION_DYNAMIC_PERSISTENT_BIT` is not exposed to them (when the docs say "_This_ flag is not exposed [...]" I meant `BUFFER_CREATION_DYNAMIC_PERSISTENT_BIT`).

If the wrong type is used (e.g. `UNIFORM_TYPE_UNIFORM_BUFFER_DYNAMIC` when the buffer is not dynamic or viceversa) Godot's validation will complain (and also Vulkan Validation Layers if our validation somehow fails).

If API users try to call buffer_update() on a dynamic buffer (that they received from Godot), this will work in the same way it works internally: Either validation complains and users cannot make that call successfully, or validation allows it (buffer_update can only be called once per frame on the same dynamic buffer).

body: Below you say "Must always be false for user-facing public API. See remarks." Which contradicts this statement.

@DarioSamo Do you think there is a way to more elegantly handle this in the RenderingDeviceGraph? I suspect that we can make it so the graph just doesn't attempt to re-order buffer_updates on dynamic buffers.

I have a few things to say. Please note that I wrote documentation about buffer_update() in general because it was lacking and it is a key place.

**When NOT using dynamic buffers:** IIRC this is also the behavior. It may have changed since I wrote it; but IIRC `buffer_updates` batches on purpose. Please note that in Vulkan and Metal, buffer_updates() -> draw_list_draw() -> buffer_updates() -> draw_list_draw() requires closing the render pass and reopening it.

"Fixing" this behavior goes against the very reason the render graph was written. I am merely documenting it so others become aware of it.

**When using dynamic buffers:** Unless someone comes up with some brilliant idea I didn't think of, dynamic buffers are **not** delaying the copy. The copy happens right when the caller calls buffer_update(). It happens before the render graph even begins reordering commands.

All solutions at "fixing" this would involve creating a temporary buffer where we copy the data, which breaks the point of UMA. The thing about dynamic buffers / UMA is that they are a highway to a fast path that is full of perils and possible bugs if assumptions are broken, which is why my code puts a ton of asserts and doesn't expose this interface to users. Making dynamic buffers "safe" negates the optimization they provide. Because the optimization lies in not being safe. We enforce safety by different ways (having debug builds validate usage and explode when they detect invalid use; safety is enforced by simply saying "don't do the unsafe thing").
